title: Mixtures
status: draft: written 18 Nov 2026 offline for Grade 5 Science and Technology; not yet checked by a CBC Science and Technology teacher; not loaded by the live tutor
notes: Real mixtures on the desk: maize and beans, sand and water, salt water, oil and water, iron filings and sand. Every separation is done or shown: picking, sieving, winnowing (outside), filtering through a cloth, decanting, using a magnet, evaporating (teacher heats).

skills.key_step: The child says a mixture is two or more substances put together that keep their own properties and can be separated again, in any amounts, made by people or by nature.

floor.prerequisite: Can sort substances into solids, liquids and gases.
floor.question: Is salt a solid, a liquid or a gas?

representations: maize and beans in a basin
salt water left to dry on a saucer
air and soil as natural mixtures
steps: Put two substances together.
Ask: is each one still there?
Can we get each one back?
Then it is a mixture, whatever the amounts.

board.do: Draw a saucer of salty water in the sun.
Ask what will be on the saucer tomorrow.
Wait for the child's prediction.
Draw salt crystals on the dry saucer.

misconceptions.ask: What was left on the dry saucer?
misconceptions.repair: A mixture can be separated again.

misconceptions.ask: Is air made of one gas or many?
misconceptions.repair: Natural things like air and soil are mixtures too.

misconceptions.ask: Is a spoon of sugar in a cup of tea still a mixture?
misconceptions.repair: A mixture can have any amounts.

misconceptions.ask: If we dry the tea, what is left?
misconceptions.repair: Dissolved sugar is still sugar.

checks.question: Is soil a mixture? Why?
checks.answer: Yes: it holds sand, clay, water and bits of plants that can be separated

checks.question: Salt is dissolved in water. Can the salt be got back?

skills.key_step: The child calls a mixture homogeneous if it looks the same all through (salt water, sugar in tea, air) and heterogeneous if the parts can be seen (soil in water, oil and water, maize and beans), whatever was done to it.

floor.question: Is tea with sugar a mixture?

representations: clear jars of salt water, muddy water and oil on water
the jars after ten minutes of standing
steps: Look at the mixture after it has stood a while.
Can you see different parts or layers?
Yes: heterogeneous. No: homogeneous.
Dissolved things are still there even if not seen.
contexts: cooking oil in a pan of water

board.do: Draw three jars: salt water, muddy water, oil on water.
Point at the oil jar.
Wait for the child to say yes.
Ask the child to label each jar homogeneous or heterogeneous.

misconceptions.ask: What did the dried saucer show?
misconceptions.repair: Dissolved salt is there; salt water is a homogeneous mixture.

misconceptions.ask: Can clear water hold dissolved salt?
misconceptions.repair: A clear liquid can still be a mixture.

listen_for: I stirred it so it is the same
misconceptions.ask: What do you see after the muddy water stands?
misconceptions.repair: Stirring does not make soil and water homogeneous.

misconceptions.ask: What happened when the oil and water stood?
misconceptions.repair: Oil and water form layers: heterogeneous.

checks.question: Is muddy water homogeneous or heterogeneous?
Is sugar dissolved in clear water homogeneous or heterogeneous?

skills.key_step: The child names a mixture by the states of its parts (solid-solid, solid-liquid, liquid-liquid, and those with gases) and gives an everyday example of each.

floor.prerequisite: Can sort substances into solids, liquids and gases.
floor.question: Is cooking oil a solid or a liquid?

representations: maize and beans, sand and water, oil and water
a table: mixture, part 1, part 2, type
steps: Name each part of the mixture.
Say the state of each part.
Join them: solid-liquid, liquid-liquid, solid-solid.
Remember gases: soda, air.

board.do: Draw a table: mixture, parts, type.
Write "muddy water" in the first row.
Point at the parts column.
board.say: What are the two parts and their states?

board.do: Wait for soil (solid) and water (liquid).
Write "solid-liquid".

misconceptions.ask: Was the salt a solid or a liquid before it dissolved?
misconceptions.repair: Salt water is a solid-liquid mixture.

misconceptions.ask: Does honey flow and take the shape of the jar?
misconceptions.repair: Thick liquids are still liquids.

misconceptions.ask: What are the bubbles in soda?
misconceptions.repair: Gases can be part of mixtures.

misconceptions.ask: What settles at the bottom?
misconceptions.repair: Name a mixture by its parts: soil and water, solid-liquid.

checks.question: What type of mixture is sand and iron filings?
Give an example of a liquid-liquid mixture.
checks.answer: oil and water, or milk and water

skills.key_step: The child chooses the method that fits the difference between the parts: size (sieving, picking), weight in the wind (winnowing), settling (decanting), particles that pass a filter (filtering), magnetism (magnet), dissolved solid (evaporation).

floor.prerequisite: Can tell homogeneous from heterogeneous mixtures.
floor.question: Is sand in water heterogeneous?

representations: a sieve, a cloth filter, a magnet and a tray
a chart: difference between parts, method
steps: Name the two parts.
Find how they differ: size, weight, magnetism, dissolving.
Pick the method that uses that difference.
Check which part you want to keep.

board.do: Write "iron filings + sand".
Point at the iron filings.
board.say: What do iron filings do that sand does not?

board.do: Wait for "a magnet pulls them".
Write "use a magnet".
Ask which method separates beans from chaff.

misconceptions.ask: Will filter paper stop dissolved salt?
misconceptions.repair: Filtering does not remove dissolved solids.

misconceptions.ask: Did the magnet lift the aluminium foil?
misconceptions.repair: A magnet pulls iron and steel only.

listen_for: use a separating funnel for sand
misconceptions.ask: What does a separating funnel separate?
misconceptions.repair: A separating funnel separates two liquids that do not mix.

misconceptions.ask: Do you want to keep the water?
misconceptions.repair: Filter or decant to keep the water.

checks.question: How would you separate small stones from rice?
checks.answer: pick them out by hand (or sieve if sizes differ)

checks.question: How do you get salt back from salt water?

skills.key_step: The child explains why a method works by naming the property it uses: the sieve lets small pieces through, the wind blows light chaff further, the filter traps undissolved bits, the magnet attracts iron, heat turns water to vapour and leaves the solid.

floor.prerequisite: Can choose a method for a mixture.
floor.question: Which method separates beans from chaff?

representations: a sieve with flour and lumps
a cloth filter over a jar
steps: Name the method.
Name the property it uses (size, weight, magnetism, dissolving).
Say what stays and what goes.
Check with a real try.

board.do: Draw a winnowing tray with grain and chaff in the air.
Point at the chaff.
board.say: Why does the wind carry the chaff further?

board.do: Wait for "it is lighter".
Write "light chaff blows away; heavy grain falls back".

listen_for: the filter takes out the salt
misconceptions.ask: Does the filtered salt water still taste salty?
misconceptions.repair: Dissolved bits pass through a filter.

misconceptions.ask: Which is lighter: the grain or the chaff?
misconceptions.repair: The wind carries the light chaff; grain falls back.

misconceptions.ask: Can the big lumps fit through the holes?
misconceptions.repair: Small pieces fall through; big ones stay on the sieve.

misconceptions.ask: Which part jumped to the magnet on its own?
misconceptions.repair: The magnet pulls the iron; sand stays.

checks.question: Why does sieving separate flour from lumps?
checks.answer: the small flour particles pass through the holes, the big lumps do not

checks.question: Why does filtering not remove sugar from water?
checks.answer: the sugar is dissolved and passes through the filter

skills.key_step: The child gives everyday uses of separation at home, on the farm and in industry (sieving flour, winnowing, straining tea, filtering water, getting salt by evaporation at the coast).
representations: a tea strainer and a sieve
a picture of salt pans at Magarini
steps: At home: straining tea, sieving flour, picking stones from rice.
On the farm: winnowing, threshing.
In industry: salt from sea water, sugar from cane.
Water: filtering is a first step, then boiling.

board.do: Draw a tea strainer over a cup.
Point at the leaves left in the strainer.
board.say: What kind of separation is this?

board.do: Wait for "filtering".
Ask the child to draw one more separation done at home.

misconceptions.ask: What does your family do with the tea leaves?
misconceptions.repair: People separate mixtures every day at home.

misconceptions.ask: Does a filter stop germs?
misconceptions.repair: Filtering removes dirt; boil or treat to kill germs.

misconceptions.ask: How is chaff removed in a windy place?
misconceptions.repair: Farmers winnow and sieve as well as pick.

misconceptions.ask: What stays on the strainer?
misconceptions.repair: A tea strainer filters the leaves from the tea.

checks.question: Give one way mixtures are separated at home.
checks.answer: straining tea, sieving flour, picking stones from rice

checks.question: How is salt got from sea water at the coast?
checks.answer: by evaporating the water in salt pans
